concepts.def: The US advanced-manufacturing production credit: a per-unit federal tax credit for domestically made battery cells, modules, and components — the incentive pulling battery manufacturing onshore.

The next-generation data-center power architecture: distributing 800-volt direct current to the rack instead of low-voltage AC. Higher voltage means lower current and losses, fewer conversion stages, and far less copper for megawatt-class racks.

Anti-dumping and countervailing duties: US trade remedies against imports priced below fair value or subsidized at home. Even a petition creates pricing risk, because duties can apply retroactively to goods already entered.

A power-generation gas turbine derived from an aircraft engine rather than designed as a heavy industrial frame. Lighter and far quicker to start than a heavy-duty machine, in blocks of roughly tens of megawatts — and because the cores can come from retiring airliners, sourceable outside the heavy-frame factory queue that sets everyone else's delivery date.

The explosive release of energy when current jumps through the air between conductors — a blast hot enough to be lethal at a panel door. An arc-flash study calculates that energy at every piece of gear so the right protective clothing and breaker settings can be specified, and it has to be redone whenever the electrical system changes.

Automatic transfer switch: the device that senses utility failure, signals the generators to start, and moves the load onto them once generation is stable — then manages the return trip when utility power comes back. It is the conductor of a data center's outage choreography.
Adding new battery capacity to an operating storage plant to offset degradation, keeping the plant at its contracted capacity over its life.

A contracted promise about the fraction of hours a plant will be ready to perform, with money attached to missing it. It matters more than an average suggests, because storage and generation revenue concentrate into a small number of extreme-price hours — a site that is available almost all year and unavailable for the wrong afternoon has not lost a proportional share of its income.

Whether lenders and investors will finance a project or accept a supplier — a function of certifications, warranties, balance-sheet strength, track record, and policy exposure rather than spec-sheet performance.

Battery backup unit: a small battery shelf inside the rack itself, carrying the servers for seconds rather than minutes — long enough to cover a transfer or ride out a disturbance. It moves the last line of stored energy from the UPS room to the point of use.

Generation or storage connected on the customer's side of the utility meter, serving the site directly — like on-site power at a data-center campus — versus front-of-the-meter assets selling into the grid.

Battery energy storage system: a grid-connected battery plant — cells packaged into modules and enclosures plus power conversion, thermal management, and controls. Rated in MW (power) and MWh (energy).

Restarting a dead network with no outside power to draw on: small units boot first to energize controls and fuel systems, then larger machines and load return in stages. Rarely exercised on the grid and definitional for an island or a microgrid, which has nothing else to start from.

Battery management system: the electronics that watch every cell's voltage, current, and temperature, balance the cells, and disconnect the battery when limits are crossed — the battery's safety and health guardian.

A site that already carries industrial infrastructure — most valuably an existing grid connection and substation from a retired plant. In a market where interconnection is the long pole, inheriting energized wires can move a project years ahead of an equivalent greenfield, which is why retired coal and industrial sites are being bought for their electrical position rather than their land.

A solid bar of copper or aluminum used instead of cable to carry very large currents over short distances inside equipment, a rack, or a switchboard. It is the same idea as facility busway one scale smaller and inside the machine, and its cross-section is the only thing standing between the current and the heat that current makes.

Prefabricated bus bar running overhead along a row of racks, with tap-off boxes that branch power down to each cabinet. It replaces bundles of individually pulled feeders, so capacity can be added or moved without rewiring — which is why the 800 VDC designs distribute at the row on busway rather than conduit.
How fast a battery charges or discharges relative to its capacity: 1C empties it in one hour, 0.25C in four. Grid storage typically runs at low C-rates — multi-hour durations rather than sprints.

Coolant distribution unit: the heat exchanger and pump station that separates the facility's water loop from the clean liquid loop feeding the servers, delivering coolant to the cold plates at the right temperature and pressure. It is the interface that lets one facility cooling spine serve many different rack designs.

A liquid-cooled metal block clamped directly onto a processor, carrying heat away in a coolant loop instead of an air stream. Above roughly 100 kW per rack air physically cannot move the heat fast enough, so liquid has to touch the silicon.
Data-center space, power, and cooling leased to tenants who bring their own IT equipment. Colocation providers are the landlords of the AI buildout.

Two heat engines on one fuel: a gas turbine burns the gas, and its hot exhaust then boils water to spin a second, steam turbine. Recovering that otherwise-wasted heat pushes modern plants past 60 percent efficiency — the highest of any gas machine — at the cost of far more equipment and a much longer build than simple cycle.

The structured testing that proves a finished plant performs as contracted before it is handed over and paid for. For storage it is where capacity and round-trip-efficiency guarantees are measured; for a data center it is where the outage choreography gets rehearsed rather than discovered in production.

One place in a power chain where electricity changes form or level — AC to DC, one DC voltage to another, one AC voltage to another. Each stage costs roughly one to three percent of the power as heat that must then be cooled, plus a box, floor space, and a way to fail; designing a power architecture is largely the art of deleting stages.

Common Redundant Power Supply: the industry-standard shape, connector, and signaling for a server power-supply module, so any compliant vendor's unit fits any compliant server. Standardizing the slot is what turns server power into a contested commodity market rather than a per-vendor design.

Being instructed to reduce output or consumption because the network cannot accommodate it at that moment. For a generator it is power that cannot be sold; for a very large load it is a contractual duty to back off — and a curtailment protocol is the document saying under what conditions, for how long, and who decides.

How many full charge-discharge cycles a cell delivers before its capacity falls to a stated fraction of new — commonly 70 or 80 percent. It is the number a storage warranty is written around, and it is quoted against specific depth-of-discharge and temperature conditions, so two figures are only comparable when those conditions match.

A converter that changes one DC voltage to another without passing through AC. It is the stage that does the work once power has arrived as direct current — inside a rack, inside a vehicle, or on a server board — and it is what lets a high-voltage DC bus feed low-voltage electronics.
The gradual loss of a battery's usable capacity with cycling and age. Storage contracts manage it with capacity guarantees and planned augmentation.

Operating equipment below its nameplate rating because real conditions — ambient temperature, altitude, state of charge, or age — do not match the conditions the rating assumed. A specification read as a guaranteed operating number rather than a rated one is one of the most common sources of a capacity shortfall that presents as an equipment fault.

A simulated copy of a real asset, fed by its live data, used to rehearse changes before they touch the hardware — testing a control strategy, forecasting degradation, or learning what normal looks like so anomalies stand out. It is how an operator tries something on a plant without trying it on the plant.
How long a storage plant can discharge at full power (energy divided by power, MWh ÷ MW). Duration decides which grid jobs a battery can do — most US grid-scale projects run a few hours.

Energy management system: the supervisory software that decides when a storage plant charges and discharges — following price signals, grid instructions, or a contract — and coordinates the PCS and BMS to do it.

The moment new electrical infrastructure is first put under live voltage and proven, with the utility present. It is the line between contracted megawatts and connected ones: before it, a connection agreement is a promise; after it, power can actually flow, and every schedule upstream of it is measured against this date.

A battery optimized for how much it holds and how many times it can be emptied and refilled — sized by hours of duration and judged on cycle life and cost per stored unit. A grid storage container is the archetype, and it is the near-inverse of a power battery in almost every design choice.
Engineering, procurement, and construction: the contractor model that delivers a plant turnkey under one contract — and the label for the firms that do it.

The Texas grid operator. An energy-only market with its own interconnection process — faster to connect, more volatile to operate in — which is why so much US storage and data-center buildout lands in Texas.

Foreign entity of concern: a US legal designation (tied to China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea) that disqualifies projects and products with too much such involvement from federal tax credits — a central bankability question for China-linked battery supply.

A resource that interconnects on the utility's side of the customer meter, like a small power plant, and is paid by wholesale markets or by contract — as opposed to behind-the-meter equipment on a customer's own site. Which side of the meter a project sits on decides the buyer, the contract, the rulebook, and the length of the sales cycle, which is why it is usually the first qualifying question asked.
Gallium nitride: a wide-bandgap semiconductor suited to very fast, compact low-to-mid-voltage converters — one of the two key materials (with SiC) shrinking modern power electronics.

Grain-oriented electrical steel: the specialty magnetic steel every transformer core requires. Only a handful of mills worldwide produce it, and every announced transformer plant bids for the same tonnage — which is why transformer lead times, not capital, gate so many projects.

An inverter that locks onto the grid's existing voltage wave and injects current into it — a surfer riding a wave someone else is making. It is the conventional mode and works well, but it cannot operate at all without a live grid to follow, so it contributes nothing during the outage it is standing beside.
An inverter that sets its own voltage and frequency like a traditional generator, rather than following the grid's. It lets storage stabilize weak grids and restart dead ones (black start).

Distortion added to a clean AC waveform by loads that draw current in gulps rather than smoothly — rectifiers, drives, server power supplies. Harmonics overheat transformers and neutral conductors, nuisance-trip breakers, and distort the voltage other equipment sees; total harmonic distortion (THD) is the score, and under 5% is the common target.

The efficiency yardstick for a thermal power plant: fuel energy in per unit of electricity out, so a lower number is better. It decides which plants a market dispatches first, hour by hour, and it is the same quantity as percentage efficiency quoted the other way up.

How long a server power supply can carry its load on internal capacitors after its input disappears — roughly 10 to 20 milliseconds. It is the physics referee for every power transfer: a switchover completed inside that window is invisible to the IT load, and one that misses it is an outage.

High-voltage direct current: moving power as DC instead of AC — over long transmission links, and now inside the data center as the 800 VDC rack architecture. Fewer conversion stages and far less copper, at the cost of protection that cannot wait for an AC waveform to cross zero and extinguish the arc for it.
One of the giant cloud and platform operators that build and lease data-center capacity at gigawatt scale. Their capital spending sets the pace of the AI data-center buildout.

Inverter-based resource: anything that reaches the grid through power electronics rather than through a spinning machine — solar, wind, and battery storage. The category exists because inverters behave differently from generators during a disturbance, so the reliability rules written for them are separate rules.

The standard that sets harmonic-distortion limits at the point of common coupling — the property line where a facility's electrical system meets the utility. It draws the boundary so one customer's distorted loads cannot degrade a neighbor's power quality, and compliance is measured at that point rather than assumed.

The technical diligence firm lenders hire to review a project on their behalf — the design, the equipment, the contracts, the production estimate. Its report is the gate to financial close, which makes the independent engineer, not the buyer, the audience a supplier's certifications and track record ultimately have to satisfy.

The stabilizing effect of heavy spinning generator masses, which resist sudden changes in grid frequency and buy operators seconds to react. As synchronous plants retire in favor of inverter-connected wind, solar, and storage, that inertia has to be replaced — by synchronous condensers, or by grid-forming inverters imitating it electronically.
The waiting line for grid-connection studies and approval. Multi-year queues are one of the main bottlenecks for new data centers and storage plants.

A converter that turns direct current into alternating current — the mirror image of a rectifier. It appears wherever DC has to be handed back to an AC world: on the output of a battery or solar array, inside a UPS, and between an electric vehicle's pack and its motor. A bidirectional one that does both jobs is a power conversion system.

Integrated resource plan: a regulated utility's commission-filed roadmap of what it expects to need and how it intends to procure it. Certified IRP megawatts are the real demand pipeline for an equipment supplier — they become purchase orders on a multi-year fuse.

Running electrically disconnected from the grid, with on-site generation alone matching the load every second. There is no larger system to lean on, so frequency and voltage become the site's own problem — and so does restarting after a total loss.
The US investment tax credit: a percentage of a storage or solar project's cost returned as a federal tax credit. A core driver of BESS project economics, with bonus tiers for domestic content.

A utility rate class written specifically for very large customers such as data centers: long contract terms, minimum-take obligations, exit fees, and collateral. It is the filter that separates real demand from speculative interconnection requests, and the instrument that turns AI load into something a utility can plan and finance against.

Lithium iron phosphate: a lithium-ion battery chemistry using an iron-phosphate cathode. It trades some energy density for lower cost, longer cycle life, and much better thermal stability than nickel-based chemistries — which is why it dominates grid-scale storage.

Long-term service agreement: the multi-year operations-and-maintenance contract through which a supplier delivers availability guarantees on the equipment it sold. Suppliers generally will not extend long-dated warranties without holding it, so the LTSA and the warranty are negotiated as one package.
Distribution-level voltage, roughly the single-digit to tens of kilovolts — the tier data centers and storage plants connect at before power is stepped down to usable levels.

A self-contained power system — generation, storage, and controls — that can run connected to the grid or islanded on its own. It is how some AI campuses get power before utility interconnection arrives.

Redundancy shorthand: N is the equipment needed to carry the load, N+1 adds one spare unit, 2N doubles everything. Data centers price reliability in these terms — more redundancy means fewer outages and more capital.

A US defense-authorization provision restricting Department of Defense battery procurement from named Chinese suppliers — the list that made "is your cell maker §154-listed?" a standard sourcing question.
A newer GPU-cloud provider renting AI compute capacity, typically growing faster than its capital base — a distinct buyer class from the hyperscalers.
The US fire-protection standard for stationary energy storage installations — spacing, enclosures, suppression, and the fire testing (UL 9540A) it references. Permitting officials work from it.

Nickel manganese cobalt: a lithium-ion cathode chemistry with higher energy density than LFP but higher cost and more thermal-runaway risk — favored where weight matters, largely displaced by LFP in stationary storage.

The ERCOT rule change setting ride-through obligations for inverter-based resources, battery storage included. It is the resource-side counterpart to NOGRR 282, which governs large electronic loads: adjacent numbers, opposite sides of the same interface, and confusing the two is a common and expensive error in a technical room.

The ERCOT rule requiring new large electronic loads — data centers of 75 MW and up — to ride through voltage and frequency disturbances instead of tripping off together. It is a load rule rather than a storage standard (those are NOGRR 245 and 272), and it is what makes buffering between the grid and the GPUs close to mandatory in Texas.
The committed purchase of a project's output — power, capacity, or storage services. Signed offtake is what turns a development pipeline into a financeable project.

Power conversion system: the bidirectional inverter of a battery plant — converts the batteries' DC to grid AC when discharging and back when charging. Its rating sets the plant's power (MW), while the batteries set its energy (MWh).
Power distribution unit: data-center gear that splits and distributes power to the racks — the branch circuits between the UPS and the servers.

The largest US regional grid operator, spanning the mid-Atlantic and parts of the Midwest — including northern Virginia's data-center corridor. Its capacity market and interconnection queue shape much of the AI data-center power story.

A battery optimized for how fast it can deliver rather than how much it holds — sized by discharge rate against a short duration, and judged on rate capability and on how well it survives sitting fully charged. A backup-supply battery is the archetype, and its design choices run opposite to an energy battery's at almost every point.

The ratio of useful power to apparent power — how much of the current a facility draws actually does work. The rest is reactive power: magnetizing current sloshing between source and load, doing nothing but occupying wires and transformers, which is why utilities bill penalties when it runs low.

A slide-in conversion tray occupying rack units and feeding the rack's own DC busbar, replacing per-server conversion with a pooled stage. Shelves are built with one more module than the load needs, so any single module can fail or be swapped while the rack keeps running.
Power purchase agreement: a long-term contract to buy a project's power or capacity at agreed terms — the bankable revenue stream that lets developers finance construction.

The North American reliability standard making ride-through mandatory for inverter-based resources, storage included — the continent-wide counterpart to what individual grid operators had already required regionally. It is the point at which ride-through capability stops being a regional differentiator and becomes a baseline everywhere.

Generation that carries a site's full load continuously, as its main source — the opposite of standby plant that sits idle until the normal supply fails. The distinction changes the machine, the air permit, and the maintenance regime, so a plant sold as prime and a plant sold as backup are different products even when the hardware looks alike.

Power usage effectiveness: total facility power divided by the power that reaches the IT equipment. A PUE of 1.0 would mean every watt went to computing; the gap above it is cooling, conversion, and lighting overhead — the industry's headline efficiency number.
A power-electronics device that turns AC into DC — the first stage of nearly every power supply, charger, and data-center power shelf.

Staying connected and operating through a grid disturbance — a voltage dip or a frequency excursion — instead of protectively disconnecting. Grid codes increasingly require it of both resources and very large loads, for a blunt reason: if everything connected trips at the first sign of trouble, a local fault becomes a system-wide one.

The share of energy put into a storage system that comes back out after conversion and thermal losses — typically in the high-80s percent range for lithium-ion. The gap is energy bought but never sold.

Starting a project far enough — by spending, or by taking delivery of equipment — to lock in the tax rules in force at that moment, even if those rules later change. It creates a cohort of owners still buying under older terms, and therefore a procurement channel whose constraints differ from everyone else's.

The 2025 Texas law setting the terms on which very large loads connect to the grid: screening-study fees and proof of site control up front, mandatory curtailment protocols, and disclosure of on-site backup generation. It is the template other states are copying, and it is what makes a data center's ability to shed or buffer load a condition of connecting at all.

Supervisory control and data acquisition: the operator's window onto a plant — live telemetry out, remote commands in. It is a visibility and intervention layer rather than a deciding one; the automated control loops below it are acting far faster than anyone is watching.

The two ways AI machines are wired together. Scale-up is the memory-speed link that makes a group of GPUs behave as one accelerator — it rides copper, so its reach is about one rack. Scale-out is the switched network between racks, with longer latency and protocol overhead, which is why so much engineering effort goes into packing more compute and more power into that single rack-sized domain.
US tariffs on Chinese imports imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act — including steep rates on lithium-ion batteries — that reshape the landed cost of China-sourced storage hardware.

Arranging breakers in series so a fault trips only the nearest device upstream of it, cutting the failure away surgically while the rest of the building keeps running. Engineers nest the devices' time-current curves so the downstream breaker always wins the race; without it, a rack-level fault can open a main breaker and darken a whole hall.

Silicon carbide: a wide-bandgap semiconductor that switches faster with lower losses than silicon, at higher voltages and temperatures — the material behind smaller, more efficient inverters and converters.

A conversion cabinet standing beside a rack that produces the rack's high-voltage DC bus from whatever the building already distributes. It is a bridge product by design: it delivers a new power architecture to one rack without rebuilding the hall around it — which is also the precise boundary of what it fixes, since the hall's upstream capacity is unchanged.

A gas turbine that drives a generator and vents its hot exhaust rather than recovering it. Cheaper, faster to build, and quick to start, but only roughly 35 to 40 percent of the fuel's energy reaches the wires — which is why it survives as a peaking and bridge machine rather than as baseload.
A battery chemistry replacing lithium with abundant sodium — cheaper materials and better cold-weather performance at lower energy density; an emerging challenger for stationary storage.

A fuel cell with a ceramic electrolyte that works only when very hot, roughly 700 to 1,000 degrees Celsius. The heat is the point: at that temperature natural gas breaks down into hydrogen right at the electrode, so the cell runs on pipeline gas rather than purified hydrogen. There is no flame, so nitrogen oxides and particulates are near zero — but the ceramics dislike being cycled and prefer steady output.

Solid-state circuit breaker: a breaker that interrupts electronically in a fraction of a millisecond, before fault current reaches its peak, instead of physically parting contacts. It is the enabling protection device for DC distribution, where there is no AC zero crossing to help extinguish the arc.

Solid-state transformer: a power-electronics replacement for the iron transformer that converts medium-voltage AC directly to regulated DC using high-frequency switching — a candidate to collapse today's multi-stage data-center power chain into one device.

The fuel gauge: how much energy is on board right now, as a percentage of what the plant can hold. Operators run a narrower window than the physical one because cells age faster held near either extreme, and every dispatch decision is planned around this number.

The long-term gauge: how much capacity a battery still holds compared with when it was new. Where state of charge moves through the day, state of health only ever falls — and how fast it falls is what a capacity warranty is a promise about.

A device storing energy as separated electric charge rather than as a chemical reaction. It holds far less energy than a battery of the same size but takes it in and gives it back within milliseconds, over and over, for many years — which makes it the right part for absorbing a spike and the wrong one for riding out an outage.

The assemblies of breakers, switches, and protective relays that route power and isolate faults at a substation or in a power room. It is where the electrical system decides which circuits go dark when something fails — and, built into factory-tested skids, it is how much of a data center's power room now arrives on site.

A large generator spinning in synchronism with the grid with no fuel and no turbine — it produces no energy, but supplies inertia, reactive power, and fault current on demand. Retired coal and gas units are being converted into them, keeping the machine and its interconnection alive to stabilize the grid that replaced it.

A contract in which the buyer pays for a committed quantity whether or not it is used. It shifts utilization risk to the buyer and turns a speculative revenue line into one lenders will underwrite — the structure behind both colocation leases and the minimum-take terms in large-load utility tariffs.

A self-accelerating overheating reaction inside a battery cell: heat triggers reactions that release more heat, potentially propagating cell to cell. The failure mode BESS safety standards are designed to contain.
A storage contract where the offtaker pays a fixed fee for the right to charge and discharge the battery as they wish — the owner operates the asset, the toller takes the market risk.

A device that changes AC voltage through two magnetically coupled windings, stepping transmission voltage down through substation, medium-voltage, and unit tiers until equipment can use it. Every step costs a little efficiency, a data-center power chain passes through several, and the lead time on large units is one of the buildout's hardest constraints.
The test method that characterizes how battery fires start and propagate at cell, module, unit, and installation level. Its data feeds fire-safety design and permitting for storage projects.
Uninterruptible power supply: a battery-backed power stage that carries the load through grid disturbances until generators start. In data centers it sits between utility power and the IT load.

The Uptime Institute's availability ladder for data centers: Tier I basic, Tier II redundant components, Tier III concurrently maintainable — any part serviceable without downtime — and Tier IV fault-tolerant, surviving any single failure. It is the shorthand buyers use for how much redundancy, and how much capital, a facility carries.

A control mode that makes a grid-forming inverter behave like a traditional spinning generator, resisting frequency change as though it had rotating mass it does not have. It is how an inverter-based plant supplies the stabilizing behavior retiring thermal plants used to provide for free, and it is what makes black start and off-grid running possible.

Voltage regulator module: the last conversion stage on the server board, stepping the rack's supply down to roughly one volt at the processor die. It is the final link in a chain of conversions running from the transmission line to the chip, and every one of them costs efficiency.

Water usage effectiveness: water consumed per unit of IT energy, the cooling counterpart to PUE. Closed-loop and air-cooled designs spend a little more electricity to spend almost no water, which in a water-stressed watershed is usually the more permittable trade.

The instant an alternating waveform passes through zero volts, twice per cycle. For a fraction of a millisecond nothing sustains an arc, so an arc drawn on AC tends to extinguish itself — and almost every protective device in an AC building quietly relies on that. Direct current never offers the instant, which is why DC protection has to be engineered rather than inherited.
